usage: I buy clothes at the store.
place + 에서 marks where an action happens
상점 + 운영하다 is the set phrase for operating a shop
주인 attaches with no particle to mean the shopkeeper
동네 (local area) is the most common modifier
examples: 상점이 많아요.
There are many stores.
simple 이/가 subject statement; 많다 = to be many
상점 앞에서 만나요.
Let's meet in front of the store.
앞에서 (in front of + at) names a meeting spot
그 상점은 물건이 좋아서 손님이 많아요.
That store has good goods, so it has many customers.
real situation: -아서 links cause (good goods) to result (many customers)
nuance: 상점 is the broad, slightly bookish word for a retail shop, built from the hanja 商店 (商 'commerce' + 店 'shop'), so it literally reads 'commerce-shop.' Its everyday rival is 가게, which is the warm, native-feeling word people actually say out loud ('동네 가게', the corner shop); 상점 sounds a notch more formal and is what you see on signs, in textbooks, and in writing. Compare also 매장, which is a brand's sales floor inside a bigger building. The English-speaker pitfall: do not stretch 상점 to cover a restaurant or a café — those are 식당 and 카페, never 상점. And because English says 'at the store,' learners reach for 에, but the location of an action takes 에서 (상점에서 사요), while 에 marks a destination or static existence (상점에 가요 / 상점에 있어요).

mistakes: Saying '상점에 옷을 사요' for 'I buy clothes at the store.' Buying is an action performed there, so it needs the action-location particle: 상점에서 옷을 사요. 에 would only fit a verb of going or existing.
Calling a restaurant a 상점. 상점 sells goods, not meals; a place you eat at is 식당 (or 음식점), and a coffee place is 카페.
Treating 상점 and 가게 as interchangeable in casual speech. They overlap in meaning, but in spoken Korean 가게 is far more natural ('가게 가서 우유 사 와'), while 상점 can sound stiff.

usage: 둘러보다 (look around) takes 매장 as its object with 을
직원 attaches directly to mean the floor employee
오프라인 distinguishes a real shop from an online one
들르다 (stop by) pairs with 에, the destination particle
examples: 매장이 넓어요.
The outlet is spacious.
simple description; 넓다 = to be wide/spacious
매장에서 옷을 입어 봐요.
I try on clothes at the outlet.
입어 보다 = 'try wearing'; 에서 marks where you do it
이 브랜드는 백화점 안에 매장이 있어요.
This brand has an outlet inside the department store.
real situation: 안에 (inside) shows a 매장 nested in a bigger building
nuance: 매장 comes from the hanja 賣場 (賣 'to sell' + 場 'place/floor'), literally 'selling-floor,' and that image is the key: it is the sales space of a brand or company, very often a counter or section housed inside a department store, mall, or large building. The near-synonym 가게 is a standalone little shop someone owns; 매장 is corporate and branch-like — Nike has 매장, your aunt has a 가게. 상점 is the generic textbook word, while 매장 specifically foregrounds the selling area itself. The English-speaker pitfall: 'outlet' in English can mean a discount store, but Korean 매장 has no discount sense at all — a discount mall is 아울렛 (a separate loanword). Also do not call a website a 매장; an online shop is 온라인 쇼핑몰 or just 쇼핑몰.

Assuming 매장 means a bargain/discount store like an English 'outlet.' A Korean discount mall is the loanword 아울렛; plain 매장 carries no cheap-price meaning.
Saying '매장에서 가요' for 'I go to the outlet.' Going is movement toward a destination, so use 에: 매장에 가요. Reserve 에서 for actions done inside it (매장에서 봐요).

usage: 확인하다 (check) takes 영업시간 as object with 을
외 (outside of) marks times the shop is closed
끝나다 (to end) pairs with 이; the day's service is over
안내 (guidance/notice) is the posted sign of opening times
examples: 영업시간이 길어요.
The business hours are long.
simple description with 이 + 길다 (to be long)
주말 영업시간은 평일과 달라요.
Weekend business hours differ from weekdays.
everyday: 와/과 다르다 = 'differs from'; note 과 after 평일
여기 영업시간이 어떻게 되세요?
What are your business hours here?
real situation: 어떻게 되세요? is the polite set phrase to ask a shop's hours
nuance: 영업시간 is the stretch of time a business is open for service, from 영업 (營業, 'operate a business': 營 'manage' + 業 'enterprise') plus 시간 (時間, 'time-interval': 時 'hour' + 間 'gap'). So the whole word reads 'business-operating time-interval.' Distinguish it from plain 시간, which is just 'time/hours' in general; 영업시간 is specifically the open-for-customers window, and its opposite edge is marked by 영업 종료 ('closing') or 영업 시작 ('opening'). A related sign word is 휴무일, the regular day off when there are no 영업시간 at all. The English-speaker pitfall: to ask the hours, English logic tempts a literal '영업시간이 뭐예요?', but Koreans say 영업시간이 어떻게 되세요? (or 몇 시까지 해요?). Also note 영업시간 is the period; the act of being open is 영업하다 ('to be open for business'), so 'Are you open now?' is 지금 영업해요?, not 지금 영업시간이에요?.

Using plain 시간 when you mean opening hours, e.g. '이 가게 시간이 어때요?' — that just asks about time vaguely. Specify 영업시간 to mean when the shop is open.
Saying '지금 영업시간이에요?' to ask if a shop is currently open. Use the verb: 지금 영업해요? ('Are you open now?'). 영업시간 names the window, not the live open/closed state.

usage: 정가 + 로 means 'at the full price', no discount
의 links 정가 to 절반 (half) for '50% off' phrasing
정가 + 표 (table/tag) is the posted sheet of fixed prices
적혀 있다 = 'is written (and stays so)' on the tag
examples: 정가가 비싸요.
The list price is expensive.
simple 이/가 statement; 비싸다 = to be expensive
정가보다 싸게 샀어요.
I bought it cheaper than the list price.
everyday: 보다 = 'than'; 싸게 (cheaply) is the adverb form of 싸다
이 책은 정가가 만 오천 원인데 할인해서 만 원에 샀어요.
This book's list price is 15,000 won, but with a discount I bought it for 10,000.
real situation: -는데 sets up contrast between 정가 and the price actually paid (에)
nuance: 정가 is the official, fixed, manufacturer-or-seller-set price printed on a product before any markdown — from the hanja 定價 (定 'to fix/decide' + 價 'price'), literally 'decided price.' Its sharp opposite within shopping is 할인가, the 'discount price,' and you will constantly hear them paired: '정가 30,000원 → 할인가 21,000원.' Do not confuse it with 가격, which is the neutral, general word for 'price' of anything; 정가 specifically claims 'this is the standard, undiscounted figure.' Related is 정찰제, a 'fixed-price system' where haggling isn't allowed. The English-speaker pitfall: 'list price' makes learners want to say 정가 is what you pay, but in Korea the figure on the receipt is often the 할인가 or 판매가 (selling price), not the 정가. Also remember to pay 'at' a price uses 로/으로 (정가로 샀어요), not 에서.

Its sharp opposite within shopping is 할인가, the 'discount price,' and you will constantly hear them paired: '정가 30,000원 → 할인가 21,000원.' Do not confuse it with 가격, the neutral, general word for 'price' of anything; 정가 specifically means the fixed, official, undiscounted figure.

'List price' makes learners want to say 정가 is what you pay, but in Korea the figure on the receipt is often the 할인가 or 판매가 (selling price), not the 정가. Also remember to pay 'at' a price uses 로/으로 (정가로 샀어요), not 에서.

mistakes: Treating 정가 as the price you actually pay. 정가 is the pre-discount sticker figure; what you hand over may be the 할인가 (discount price) or 판매가 (selling price).
Swapping 정가 for the all-purpose 가격. 가격 just means 'price' in general; choose 정가 only when you specifically mean the fixed, official, undiscounted price.
Saying '정가에서 샀어요' for 'I bought it at list price.' The price you transact at takes 로/으로: 정가로 샀어요. 에서 would wrongly mark a location.

usage: to pay with a gift certificate
으로 marks the means of payment; 결제하다 = to settle payment
문화 (culture) + 상품권 is the popular book/media voucher brand type
to give a gift certificate as a present
선물하다 (to gift) takes 상품권 as its object with 을
권 here is the counter-suffix for the bill's face value
examples: 상품권이 있어요.
I have a gift certificate.
simple existence with 이 + 있다
상품권으로 계산했어요.
I paid with the gift certificate.
everyday: 으로 = 'by means of'; 계산하다 = to pay/check out
백화점 상품권은 현금처럼 쓸 수 있어서 선물로 인기가 많아요.
Department-store gift certificates can be used like cash, so they're popular as gifts.
real situation: 처럼 (like) + -ㄹ 수 있다 (can) explain why it's a favored 선물
nuance: 상품권 is a prepaid voucher you spend like cash at shops, from the hanja 商品券 (商品 'merchandise/goods' + 券 'ticket, certificate'), literally 'goods-ticket.' That final 권 (券) is the same 'ticket/coupon' morpheme in 입장권 (admission ticket) and 할인권 (discount coupon), so recognizing it unlocks a whole family of words. Distinguish 상품권 from 쿠폰, a coupon that knocks a percentage or amount off — a 상품권 carries real stored money you redeem, whereas a 쿠폰 just discounts. Culturally, gifting 상품권 (especially 백화점 상품권 and 문화상품권) is extremely common and not seen as impersonal. The English-speaker pitfall: don't confuse it with 영수증 (receipt) or 보증서 (warranty card); only 상품권 holds spendable value. And to pay with one, use 으로 (상품권으로 샀어요), the instrument particle — not 로 after a consonant-final noun mistakenly, since 상품권 ends in ㄴ and correctly takes 으로.

From the hanja 商品券 (商品 'merchandise/goods' + 券 'ticket, certificate'), literally 'goods-ticket.' That final 권 (券) is the same 'ticket/coupon' morpheme in 입장권 (admission ticket) and 할인권 (discount coupon), so recognizing it unlocks a whole family of words.

Writing '상품권로 샀어요.' Because 상품권 ends in the consonant ㄴ, the instrumental particle is 으로: 상품권으로 샀어요.

usage: 교환 + 하다 turns the noun into the verb 'to swap an item'
가능하다 (be possible) pairs with 이; the standard shop phrasing
로 marks what you swap into (the target size)
및 (and, formal) is the set sign wording at counters
examples: 교환이 돼요?
Can I exchange it?
simple: 되다 here means 'is allowed/possible'
이 옷을 큰 걸로 교환하고 싶어요.
I'd like to exchange this for a bigger one.
everyday: 걸로 (= 것으로) marks the replacement; -고 싶다 = 'want to'
영수증이 있어야 교환할 수 있어요.
You can exchange it only if you have the receipt.
real situation: -아야 (only if) states the condition for 교환
nuance: 교환 means swapping a purchased item for a different size, color, or model of the same kind of product, from the hanja 交換 (交 'to cross/mutual' + 換 'to change'), literally 'mutually change.' The crucial shopping contrast is with 반품, a 'return' that gives your money back: 교환 keeps the transaction (you walk out with goods), 반품 undoes it (you walk out with a refund). Counters typically post '교환·반품 안내' together. Note 교환 is also used more broadly than shopping — 의견 교환 (exchanging opinions), 정보 교환 (exchanging information) — so the word isn't shop-only, but here it's the item-swap sense. The English-speaker pitfall: English 'exchange money' tempts a literal 돈을 교환하다, but currency exchange is 환전 (a different word). To swap into the replacement item, use 로/으로 (큰 사이즈로 교환), and remember the verb is 교환하다, so 'I want to exchange' is 교환하고 싶어요, not 교환을 싶어요.

mistakes: Confusing 교환 (swap for another item) with 반품 (return for a refund). If you want your money back, that's 반품; 교환 means you leave with replacement goods.
Saying 돈을 교환하다 for changing currency. Money exchange is 환전(하다); 교환 is for swapping purchased items or, figuratively, opinions/information.
Marking the replacement with the wrong particle: '큰 사이즈에 교환해요.' Use 로/으로 for what you swap into — 큰 사이즈로 교환해요.

usage: 반품 + 하다 forms the verb 'to send goods back'
가능하다 pairs with 이; the policy-statement phrasing
신청 (application) + 반품 is the online button to start a return
return due to a change of mind
단순 변심 ('simple change of heart') is the fixed policy term
examples: 반품이 돼요?
Can I return it?
simple: 되다 = 'is allowed', the quick counter question
이 신발을 반품하고 환불받고 싶어요.
I'd like to return these shoes and get a refund.
everyday: -고 chains 반품하다 and 환불받다 (receive a refund)
택을 떼면 반품이 안 되니까 조심하세요.
If you remove the tag, a return isn't possible, so be careful.
real situation: -니까 gives the reason warning before acting
nuance: 반품 is sending a purchased item back to the seller, normally to undo the sale and get a refund, from the hanja 返品 (返 'to send back/return' + 品 'goods'), literally 'return the goods.' The sharp pair is 교환 (swap for another item, transaction kept) versus 반품 (give it back, transaction reversed) — Korean shops list them side by side as '교환·반품.' Closely linked is 환불 (還拂, 'refund'): you do a 반품 in order to receive a 환불, so they often appear together (반품하고 환불받다). The English-speaker pitfall: English 'return to the store' can make learners think of going back to a place, but 반품 is about returning the goods, not yourself returning somewhere — physically going back is 돌아가다, while handing the item back is 반품하다. Also, 반품하다 already contains 하다, so don't add an extra verb: 'I returned it' is 반품했어요, not 반품을 했어요 in the sense of doing something else.

structuredNuance.t: 반품 is sending a purchased item back to the seller, normally to undo the sale and get a refund.

The sharp pair is 교환 (swap for another item, transaction kept) versus 반품 (give it back, transaction reversed) — Korean shops list them side by side as '교환·반품.' Closely linked is 환불 (還拂, 'refund'): you do a 반품 in order to receive a 환불, so they often appear together (반품하고 환불받다).
From the hanja 返品 (返 'to send back/return' + 品 'goods'), literally 'return the goods.'

English 'return to the store' can make learners think of going back to a place, but 반품 is about returning the goods, not yourself returning somewhere — physically going back is 돌아가다, while handing the item back is 반품하다. Also, 반품하다 already contains 하다, so don't add an extra verb: 'I returned it' is 반품했어요.

mistakes: Mixing up 반품 (return for refund) and 교환 (swap for a different item). If you want money back, say 반품; 교환 leaves you with replacement goods.
Using 반품 for 'returning to a place.' 반품 means sending goods back; physically going back somewhere is 돌아가다. 'I'm going back to the store' is 가게에 다시 가요, not 가게에 반품해요.
Confusing 반품 with 환불. 반품 is the act of sending the item back; 환불 is getting the money. The sequence is 반품한 뒤에 환불받아요 — you return it, then you're refunded.

usage: 품절 + 되다 makes the passive 'to sell out' (no human agent)
품절 modifies 상품 (product) directly, like an adjective
임박 ('imminent') is the urgency tag on shopping sites
examples: 이거 품절이에요.
This is sold out.
simple 이에요 statement after a consonant-final noun
그 색깔은 벌써 품절됐어요.
That color is already sold out.
everyday: 품절되다 + 벌써 ('already') stresses how fast it went
사고 싶었는데 품절이라서 못 샀어요.
I wanted to buy it, but it was sold out, so I couldn't.
real situation: -이라서 ('because it is') gives the reason for 못 사다
nuance: 품절 describes a product that is completely sold out and currently unavailable, from the hanja 品切 (品 'goods' + 切 'cut off/run out'), literally 'goods cut off.' The natural opposites/relatives are 재고 ('stock on hand') and 입고 ('arrival of new stock'); a thing is 품절 precisely when the 재고 hits zero, and it returns when 재입고 (restock) happens. Distinguish 품절 from 매진 (賣盡, 'sold out'), which carries the same idea but is used for tickets and seats (콘서트 매진, a sold-out concert) rather than store merchandise — say 품절 for products, 매진 for tickets. The English-speaker pitfall: 품절 is a noun/state, and Koreans most often state it as 품절이에요 or with the verb 품절되다 (품절됐어요), so avoid forcing the English passive into something like 품절돼졌어요. usage: to have stock / be in stock
있다 with 이 is the core 'we have it' phrase
확인하다 takes 재고 as object with 를; the staff's action
떨어지다 ('fall/run out') idiomatically means stock is depleted
정리 ('sorting out') + 세일 names an inventory-clearing sale
examples: 재고가 있어요.
It's in stock.
simple existence: 이 + 있다 = 'there is stock'
이 사이즈 재고가 남아 있어요?

everyday: 남아 있다 ('remain') is how shoppers ask if any is left
창고에 재고가 없어서 주문해야 해요.
There's no stock in the warehouse, so we have to order it.
real situation: -아서 gives the reason; -아야 하다 = 'have to'
nuance: 재고 is the quantity of goods a shop currently has on hand to sell, from the hanja 在庫 (在 'to exist/be present' + 庫 'storehouse'), literally 'present in the warehouse.' It is the direct counterpart of 품절: while stock 재고 remains, you can buy; when 재고 runs out, the item becomes 품절. A common collocation is the idiom 재고가 떨어지다 ('stock runs out,' literally 'falls'), the same 떨어지다 used for running out of supplies generally. usage: 를 + 주세요 is the polite 'please give me' request
나오다 ('come out') is how a bill is said to be issued
확인하다 takes 계산서 as object; you verify the amounts
좀 softens the request; 보여 주다 = 'show'
examples: 계산서 주세요.
The bill, please.
simple: drop the particle in casual speech for a quick ask
계산서가 좀 이상해요.
The bill seems a bit off.
everyday: 좀 ('a bit') + 이상하다 (be strange) flags a possible error
계산서를 보니까 음료가 두 번 찍혀 있었어요.
When I looked at the bill, the drink was rung up twice.
real situation: -니까 ('upon doing') leads into the discovery
nuance: 계산서 is the itemized statement of what you owe, from 계산 (計算, 'calculation/reckoning': 計 'to count' + 算 'to compute') plus the suffix 서 (書, 'written document'), so it reads 'a written reckoning.' That 서 (書) 'document' morpheme also forms 신청서 (application form) and 보증서 (warranty), a handy pattern to learn. The key contrast is with 영수증 (領收證, 'receipt'): a 계산서 is the request for payment showing the itemized total before/at paying, while 영수증 is the proof you already paid — at a restaurant you get the 계산서 to settle, then the 영수증 afterward. Note 계산서 also has a formal tax sense (세금계산서, 'tax invoice') in business. The English-speaker pitfall: 'bill' in English also means paper money, but Korean 계산서 never means a banknote — a bill/note of money is 지폐. And to ask for the check politely, Koreans say 계산서 주세요 or simply 계산할게요 ('I'll pay'), not a literal 'check, please.'

usage: 에 marks the destination; 담다 = to put/pack into a container
비닐 (vinyl) + 봉지 is the everyday convenience-store bag
하나 (one) + 주세요; you often pay extra for it
봉지 doubles as a counter: 'a packet of'
examples: 봉지 주세요.
A bag, please.
simple request; particle dropped in casual speech
비닐봉지는 돈을 내야 해요.
You have to pay for a plastic bag.
everyday: -아야 하다 ('have to') reflects Korea's paid-bag rule
산 물건을 봉지에 담아서 들고 갔어요.
I packed what I bought into a bag and carried it out.
real situation: 담아서 ('pack and then') chains into 들고 가다 (carry along)
nuance: 봉지 is a thin plastic or paper bag for carrying purchases, and it doubles as a counter for packeted goods (과자 한 봉지, 'a bag of chips'). The most common compound is 비닐봉지 ('vinyl/plastic bag'). Crucially, distinguish 봉지 from 가방: a 가방 is a durable bag you own and reuse — a handbag, backpack, or suitcase — whereas a 봉지 is the flimsy throwaway sack the cashier gives you; calling your backpack a 봉지 sounds odd. Also nearby is 봉투, which is more for envelopes and sturdier paper/shopping bags (종이봉투), with some overlap. Culturally, Korean shops charge for 비닐봉지 by law, so 봉지 드릴까요? ('Shall I give you a bag?') usually implies a small fee. The English-speaker pitfall: English 'bag' covers everything, so learners over-apply 봉지; reserve it for disposable shopping sacks, and use 가방 for personal bags. To pack items 'into' it, use 에 with 담다 (봉지에 담다), the destination particle, not 에서.

usage: 받다 takes 거스름돈 as object with 을; you get it back
주다 hands the change to the customer; the everyday verb pairing
됐어요 ('it's fine') politely declines the change
잔돈 is the shorter near-synonym, also meaning loose coins
examples: 거스름돈 주세요.
Please give me my change.
simple request; particle dropped casually
거스름돈이 모자라요.
The change is short.
everyday: 모자라다 ('be insufficient') flags a shortfall
만 원을 냈는데 거스름돈을 안 줬어요.
I paid with 10,000 won, but they didn't give me the change.
real situation: -는데 contrasts paying with not receiving change
nuance: 거스름돈 is the money handed back when you pay more than the exact price — pure native Korean, from the verb 거스르다 ('to give change back; to go against the flow') plus 돈 ('money'), so it pictures money 'flowing back' to you. Its close synonym is 잔돈, but the two differ: 거스름돈 is specifically the change returned from a payment, while 잔돈 more broadly means small coins/loose change you carry (잔돈 있어요? = 'Do you have small change?'). From a customer's side it pairs with 받다 (거스름돈을 받다, 'receive change'); from the cashier's side it pairs with 주다 (거스름돈을 줬어요, 'gave the change') — note you say 거스름돈을 주다, not the redundant 거스름돈을 거슬러 주다, since the noun and the verb 거슬러 주다 both come from 거스르다 and stacking them doubles the meaning. The English-speaker pitfall: English 'change' is overloaded, and learners confuse this money sense with 바꾸다 ('to change/alter') or 환전 (currency exchange) — 거스름돈 has nothing to do with those. Also beware 용돈, which sounds vaguely similar but means 'pocket money/allowance,' a completely different word. To say 'keep the change,' don't translate literally; Koreans say 거스름돈은 됐어요 or 그냥 가지세요.
